I used to be a defense attorney, and hopefully sometime after the Third American Revolution, I'll be a law professor at some university somewhere. So if you'll indulge me for a minute, I'd like to put on my "law professor" hat. I am happy to teach if you're willing to listen with an open mind.

To begin with, many of the amendments in the Bill of Rights dovetail with one another; they form a sort of symbiosis of rights. In this case, we are dealing with the interplay of Amendments IV and I.

As you know, the Fourth Amendment deals with warrants. It states that

The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated; and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

Let's unpack this a little bit. The Fourth Amendment was written in response to a very evil practice of the British government called "General Warrants", which basically allowed the Redcoats to go door-to-door and search people's houses for contraband or wanted individuals, "because fucketh thee, that's why". Surely you can understand why that's a bad thing.

So the warrant requirement in the second clause has several protections baked right into it:

no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause

This means that in order for a warrant to be issued, the authorities need to have "probable cause" to believe that a crime has been committed. "Probable cause" is more than a generalized suspicion. (There's case law which fleshes all of this out, but I don't have my spellbook handy to cite it, so you'll have to trust me, sorry about that.) And while "incitement to riot" is a crime, planning a protest march is not.

supported by Oath or affirmation

This bit isn't really relevant here, so we'll leave it for now.

and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

This bit is called the "particularity" clause. Not only do the authorities have to have probable cause to believe that a crime has been committed, they have to be able to describe with particularity what they're looking for. Again, case law defines exactly what that means, but generally they do have to be pretty specific. "Any and all records from your website" absolutely does not cut it.

The reason the Fourth Amendment doesn't allow the government to go on fishing expeditions--which is exactly what this is--is because innocent people are going to get swept up in it. I'm sure there are nasty characters who visited that website, but there are many others--probably most others, to be honest--who also visited the website, but are not guilty of any crime. Those people don't deserve to be investigated; and that's why the Fourth Amendment is written the way it is.

Where the First Amendment comes into play is the "assembly" clause. Professor Eugene Volokh (who, in my opinion, is one of the best Constitutional scholars in the country, despite him having sold out to the Bezos Post) explains it better than I do:

Assembly is the only right in the First Amendment that requires more than a lone individual for its exercise. One can speak alone; one cannot assemble alone. Moreover, while some assemblies occur spontaneously, most do not. For this reason, the assembly right extends to preparatory activity leading up to the physical act of assembling, protections later recognized by the Supreme Court as a distinct “right of association,” which does not appear in the text of the First Amendment.

People have the right to associate freely and peaceably with one another, but if they might be subjected to general warrants just on the grounds of them having so associated, then they'll understandably be reluctant to exercise the right. This is called a "chilling effect", and our Courts take a very dim view of those. (Insert another punt to case law.) Again--to be fair--some people who visited the website probably had evil intent, but many didn't; and the government shouldn't discourage people from peaceably associating with one another through an implicit threat of them being investigated for it.

In summary, the warrant is way too broad. It's unconstitutionally broad. If the government has probable cause to believe that certain people visited the website, then by all means it should issue a warrant which particularly describes what and who it is looking for. It should not issue a general warrant.
